summary:
COSMIC Space Blink AI is a free, publicly accessible web application developed to make NASA's SPHEREx infrared survey data easier to explore and analyze. It enables users to select any region of the sky by object name or celestial coordinates and blink, compare, and subtract real SPHEREx images captured during different survey passes to identify moving and variable celestial objects, including brown dwarfs, nearby stars, asteroids, and variable stars.

The platform integrates automated image processing, moving-object detection, Gaia DR3 and SIMBAD catalogue cross-matching, and AstroAnalytics tools for generating light curves, spectra, and astrometric measurements. It also features Cosmo, an AI-powered assistant that helps users understand SPHEREx data, and a dedicated Planet X Lab for testing hypothetical planet detectability using clearly labeled simulations.

COSMIC directly addresses the NASA Space Apps Challenge by transforming complex astronomical datasets into an interactive and accessible discovery platform. Its importance lies in democratizing access to real space science data, supporting citizen science, and enabling researchers, students, and astronomy enthusiasts to investigate the dynamic infrared universe without specialized software.
details:
COSMIC Space Blink AI


1. What does the project do, and how does it work?

COSMIC Space Blink AI is a public-facing astronomical exploration and analysis platform developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 under the challenges Planet X and SPHEREx. It transforms NASA's SPHEREx infrared survey archive into an interactive environment where users can explore how celestial objects move and change over time.

NASA's SPHEREx mission observes the entire sky approximately every six months across 102 infrared wavelength channels, covering 0.75–5 micrometers. COSMIC allows users to search for any region of the sky using an astronomical object's name or its Right Ascension (RA) and Declination (Dec). Users can select a field of view between 2 and 20 arcminutes and retrieve real observations from the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA).

The platform processes images from different survey passes through background subtraction, bad-pixel masking, image alignment, and inverse-variance stacking. Its Blink Explorer enables users to blink, swipe, view side-by-side comparisons, and generate difference images to reveal objects that move or change brightness. An automated detection algorithm identifies potential movers by comparing positive and negative signals in difference images while rejecting stationary sources and image artifacts.

COSMIC also integrates SIMBAD and Gaia DR3 catalogues to identify known objects and account for their proper motion. Its AstroAnalytics module provides aperture photometry, light curves, infrared spectra, and astrometric measurements. The Discovery Log allows users to record, measure, and cross-match unidentified candidates.

Additionally, the platform features Cosmo, an AI-powered assistant that explains the interface and answers SPHEREx-related questions using cited mission documentation. The dedicated Planet X Lab performs injection-recovery experiments by introducing clearly labeled simulated objects into copies of real SPHEREx images to evaluate the detectability of hypothetical distant planets.

2. What benefits does it have?

COSMIC makes complex astronomical observations accessible through an integrated, browser-based platform, eliminating the need for users to independently download, process, and analyze large astronomical datasets.

Its major benefits include:

  • Automated object detection: Helps identify moving celestial sources that might otherwise remain unnoticed in large astronomical image archives.
  • Multi-epoch image comparison: Makes subtle positional and brightness variations easier to investigate.
  • Scientific analysis: Provides light curves, spectra, photometry, and astrometric measurements within one application.
  • Catalogue integration: Cross-matches potential detections with Gaia DR3 and SIMBAD to distinguish known objects from unidentified candidates.
  • AI-assisted learning: Cosmo helps students, researchers, and astronomy enthusiasts understand astronomical observations and navigate the platform.
  • Hypothesis testing: Planet X Lab provides a controlled environment for investigating detection sensitivity without presenting simulated objects as actual discoveries.
  • Efficient data access: Optimized image cutouts, parallel processing, and caching reduce repeated data retrieval and processing time.

    3. What is the intended impact of the project?

Our goal is to contribute to the exploration of the dynamic infrared universe by making astronomical data more accessible, understandable, and scientifically useful.

COSMIC has the potential to support the investigation of nearby stars, brown dwarfs, asteroids, variable stars, and other moving or changing celestial sources. By combining automated image analysis with catalogue cross-matching and scientific measurement tools, it can help researchers and citizen scientists investigate potential candidates more efficiently.

We also aim to encourage students and early-career researchers to engage with real NASA mission data, develop practical astronomical data-analysis skills, and participate in scientific exploration.

An important part of our intended impact is promoting responsible scientific investigation. COSMIC distinguishes between real NASA observations, derived measurements, catalogue information, and simulated experiments. Unmatched objects are labelled as candidates requiring further investigation rather than confirmed discoveries. This approach encourages transparency, reproducibility, and scientific integrity.


4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

We developed COSMIC using a combination of modern web-development technologies, scientific Python libraries, astronomical databases, and AI integration.

Frontend development:

  • React 19
  • TypeScript
  • Vite
  • Tailwind CSS
  • Aladin Lite for interactive astronomical sky maps
  • Plotly for scientific visualization

Backend development and scientific computing:

  • Python 3.11+
  • FastAPI for backend APIs
  • NumPy and SciPy for numerical computation and image processing
  • Astropy for astronomical calculations and coordinate handling
  • Redis and disk-based caching
  • Parallel processing and background jobs for efficient data retrieval and analysis

Astronomical data sources and integrations:

  • NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA) – real SPHEREx observations
  • ESA Gaia DR3 – stellar positions and proper motion
  • SIMBAD – astronomical object identification
  • VizieR, DSS2, 2MASS, and AllWISE—astronomical catalogue and sky-map information

Artificial intelligence:

  • Cosmo, an integrated AI assistant connected to SPHEREx documentation through a secure server-side service, providing contextual assistance and source-cited answers.

Testing and development:

  • 133 automated backend tests using synthetic images and offline testing.
  • Frontend type-checking and production builds.
  • Manual testing across desktop, tablet, and mobile layouts.

The project does not require specialized astronomical hardware from the user. It is designed to operate through a standard web browser, with Python and Node.js development environments on the backend and frontend, respectively.

5. How is the project creative and innovative?

The creativity of COSMIC lies in bringing multiple astronomical investigation techniques together into one accessible platform rather than limiting the experience to displaying telescope images.

Its central innovation is the combination of interactive multi-epoch image blinking and automated difference-image analysis. By comparing observations from different dates, stationary stars can be suppressed while moving sources become more apparent. The platform further strengthens this approach through detector-specific processing, proper-motion corrections, and catalogue cross-matching.

Another distinctive feature is the integration of scientific analysis directly into the exploration experience. Users can move from identifying a potential object to measuring its position, studying its brightness variations, examining its infrared spectrum, and recording it for further investigation without switching between separate applications.

The Planet X Lab introduces another creative dimension through injection-recovery testing. Instead of claiming to have found a hypothetical planet, it allows users to investigate whether an object with specified brightness and motion characteristics could be detected under actual SPHEREx observational conditions.

Finally, Cosmo makes the platform more interactive by connecting AI-assisted explanations with astronomical documentation and the user's exploration workflow.
6. What factors did your team consider during development?

Our team considered several scientific, technical, and accessibility-related factors to ensure that COSMIC would be useful, reliable, and scientifically responsible.

Scientific accuracy: SPHEREx uses linear variable filters, meaning wavelengths vary across the detector. We therefore considered detector-specific comparisons to avoid interpreting wavelength differences as genuine brightness changes.

Data integrity: We ensured that real NASA observations, derived measurements, catalogue information, and simulated data are clearly distinguished. Simulations never modify the original astronomical observations.

Detection reliability: We considered stationary-star rejection, bad-pixel flags, image artifacts, source blending, saturation, and cross-detector consistency. Potential detections are treated as candidates requiring verification.

Performance and scalability: We implemented smaller image cutouts, parallel processing, background jobs, and Redis/disk caching to improve retrieval speed and reduce unnecessary data transfers.

Accessibility and usability: We designed a browser-based interface with interactive visualizations, guided exploration, responsive layouts, and an AI assistant to accommodate users with different levels of astronomical experience.

Transparency and limitations: We considered the sensitivity limitations of SPHEREx observations, particularly for very faint or slowly moving objects. The platform reports unsuccessful or partial detections honestly rather than generating misleading confidence scores.

Team collaboration: Development was divided across five complementary roles: scientific analysis, backend development, image processing, frontend development, and AI engineering. This allowed us to integrate scientific reasoning, software engineering, and user-centered design into one project.

Through these considerations, we developed COSMIC Space Blink AI as an integrated astronomical exploration platform that combines real NASA data, automated scientific analysis, and responsible AI to make the discovery process more accessible to everyone.
